rationale: Parkinson and other human diets include canola or rapeseed alongside other exposures, without isolating the refined oil. The MS diet with canola advice yielded an inconclusive unadjusted fatigue comparison alongside a favorable original abstract result. The trial oil grade and the independent Parkinson fatigue direction remain unresolved.

Both arms of a Parkinson diet trial contained cinnamon. A separate distilled three-herb trial in multiple sclerosis reported a group-by-time fatigue effect and inconsistent table details. The endometriosis capsule registration gives no fatigue results. Ground cinnamon itself has no verified Parkinson fatigue comparison.

Mean fatigue rose 3.7 points in 14 Parkinson study completers after brewed green tea. The uncontrolled study supports a minimal worsening lean, with no paired data or exact p value in the same-cohort thesis. Non-Parkinson postoperative and mixed-diet studies give favorable or inconclusive fatigue findings but differ in setting and exposure. The MS diet allowed green or white tea without isolating it.

Topical ground clove and topical eugenol studies report dental pain relief. Ground clove powder in mice gave an inconclusive analgesia comparison. Isolated oral eugenol in a nerve injury model changed one thermal response but not mechanical responsiveness at observable depth. Neither result identifies a clinical direction for ingested ground clove and Parkinson pain.
